prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep B037 as my sole preferred part. The idea is specific and separable from earlier prizes: Katori's proposal that neutral atoms held in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength can be interrogated in large numbers without a light-shift penalty, followed by its realisation and the push of strontium lattice clocks to the 10^-18 regime, with many-body and comb-linked extensions from Ye's group. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories and has delivered centimetre-scale gravitational-redshift tests, bounds on varying constants and ultralight dark-matter couplings. The credit divides into two identifiable contributions without strain. Having read the full exchange, the weak points raised against B037 are about perception and timing, not about whether the achievement is real, whereas the weak points against B042 and B006 concern who should be named. The committee's task is to identify the discovery and then the people, and for B037 both steps can be done defensibly. My position on the chair's question about the 2005 prize is that the premise should be withdrawn: Hall and Hansch were the 2005 laureates, Ye was not, and his association with the comb circle is not a bar to recognition.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is novelty against recent AMO precedent (2005 comb, 2012 ion control) and the clustering of atomic and precision-measurement prizes, and I cannot fully dispose of it as a theorist; I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for the experimental priority history. Pearce and Mehlig press the question of what new principle the clock adds beyond the magic-wavelength idea. My answer is that the principle is the magic-wavelength condition itself, which removes the trade-off between many-atom statistics and systematic shifts, but I accept that this is closer to an enabling invention than to a new phenomenon, and a member who weighs new classes of matter above new measurement regimes will legitimately rate it lower. A second objection is that NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other lattice-clock groups, and the Al+ ion groups, are left outside two names, which the citation must acknowledge by being narrow. A third is whether Ye is best credited for the clock itself or for clock-comb integration and the accuracy frontier; I think the citation should state the former.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair and preferring B042, accepts that the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is a compromise rather than a complete account because of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D work, and he and Eriksson ask whether the 2016 prize overlaps with quantum spin Hall.
responses.response: On the 2016 overlap I still think time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulators are a distinct idea from the Chern-number-based phases honoured then, so I would not count adjacency as decisive against B042. My difficulty is the credit. Pearce's own wording, a trio that is a defensible compromise, is an admission that the committee would be naming three people for a field whose experimental half rests on a proposal by someone who cannot now be recognised. For a prize that must stand for a long time I weigh that more than the scientific quality, which I rate highly. I am not moved by the argument that Zhang's death makes the omission permanent and therefore tolerable; if anything that argues against fixing the line this year. I also thank him for correcting the 2005 premise, which removes one of the perception problems around B037.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B042 for its direct chain from the Z2 classification to the HgTe observation, supported by band-inversion calculations, but concedes that edge quantisation is less clean than in the quantum Hall effect and that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang cannot be repaired later.
responses.response: I agree with the strength of the idea-to-observation chain and with his own two caveats; the less clean quantisation of the helical edge is, to me, the more serious scientific point, because the headline experimental signature is weaker than the theory suggests. Where I differ is on how to weigh it against B037. His second caveat, the unrepairable omission, is the same kind of problem I would face if I tried to defend a B006 trio. I would ask him whether a citation naming the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation, and nothing else, would in his view survive the objection that the proposal the experiment tested lies elsewhere. If the answer is that it would, I would take B042 as a serious second choice, and I keep it first among my alternatives.

responses.point: Kroll values B037 as a bounded breakthrough with Katori for the concept and Ye for accuracy, coherence and systematic control, and notes that the pending redefinition of the second is prospective and that groups at JILA/NIST, PTB and RIKEN also hold priority on specific 1e-18 results.
responses.response: I agree with the division of credit and with his candour about his own taste for measurement breakthroughs, which I try to apply to myself too. On the redefinition, I read it as confirmation of maturity: the evidence behind it is the demonstrated accuracy and independent agreement of clocks, which exist regardless of a metrology decision. On Ye, his wording of the contribution as accuracy and systematic control plus comb integration is more careful than mine, and I would build the citation on the lattice clock reaching 10^-18 so that it does not read as a general prize for optical clocks or for the comb. I accept his point that priority on individual uncertainty records is shared among laboratories; that is a reason for narrow wording, not for waiting.

responses.point: Mehlig asks what new physical principle the optical lattice clock adds beyond the magic-wavelength idea, and still prefers B005 for its conceptual novelty, while acknowledging that Yuhai Tu's omission is a real defect.
responses.response: The principle question is fair and I have tried to answer it above: the magic-wavelength condition is the new element and it is what lets many neutral atoms behave as a clock without a systematic penalty. I concede it is an enabling idea and not a new phase of matter. On B005, I find the Mermin-Wagner evasion in Toner-Tu a real insight, but his own acknowledgment that Tu cannot be named, together with contested exponents and no other member preferring it, means I cannot move to it. I ask only that the committee not treat the lack of a new phase as disqualifying when the idea changes what can be measured and tested in fundamental physics.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, given that the new principle is the magic-wavelength condition.
Whether Ye is best credited for the clock itself or for clock-comb integration, and how much weight the NIST, PTB, SYRTE, RIKEN and ion-clock groups deserve.
Whether B042 could be defended in a form that survives the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission, and how much the 2016 prize and the less clean helical-edge quantisation weigh against it.
Whether any expert view could give B006 a principled three-person form; without one I do not see it as a person-based prize this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, my early mentor Hector Rubinstein, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group, and none is among the credited names on the shortlisted ballots. My field is theoretical high-energy physics and cosmology, so I have no proximity to the lattice clock, but I rely on colleagues for its experimental priority history. No disclosure has changed since round 1.
